lines.text: Barge alongside at slack, and slack's an hour off.
She'll not come in on a running tide, not with sixty ton in her. Mirefin out in barrels, flour and nails and rope in, and I've eaten out of every barrel that's crossed this dock.
You try putting sixty ton alongside on a running tide.
I keep off the third piling now when she comes alongside. Sixty ton onto soft timber.
Half the barrels we put out before. There'll be no new piling driven this year.
Came alongside at slack and the deck never moved under her.
New timber on the third piling and the fourth. First these boards have had in eleven years. My boot still goes down where the soft one used to be.
Coarse mesh for the grown Mirefin, fine for the Bogling. Summer mesh on the end rail for the Reedrick, and that one hangs dry three quarters of the year. I've taken it down a gauge since.
Water's colder than it was when I started. There's nothing more to it than that. What comes up comes up smaller because the water's colder.
The mesh follows the water. It followed the water when I started on these boards and it will do it after me.
Sel says don't trail your hand over the side. I do it anyway when he's poling.
Clause four says channel. Channel's the deep bit. It's why the boats go out where they go out.
My auntie Hetty went quiet at her supper when I said it. Then she said it back to me herself, only slower, and I said it again after her.
I'm not going to talk about my mother.
She cut the mark on my post, the second one past the steps, and the water comes up to it and does not go over.
Same mark in a drought year and the same mark in a flood year. My nephew has it that I cut a new one and forgot which, and there is no new one on that post.
I buy the season here for an office that is not in this town. The schedule comes down in the first week of the year and I price against it.
Clause four says channel. It does not say shallows and it does not say marsh, and it has stood unamended for sixty years.

People bring me marsh figures every spring. Fenmaw take Mirefin, and Mirefin is the animal the contract is written on, so the marsh figures go in the file and I price off the channel, because clause four says channel.
The warden walked that marsh again last month. She could not put a second Fenmaw in it.
Mirefin come up thick with nothing taking them and then the channel goes empty. There is a clause for that and it has been in the contract longer than I have, and it sets the price low.
Mind the wet plank. In you get, sit anywhere you like. She's steadier than she looks and no slower than his.
People stand on that bank a quarter of an hour waiting for Sel's boat rather than get in with me, and I have stopped minding that, or near enough.
Channel's on your left going out, shallows on your right. I'll point out the idol as we pass it — it's out where the reed thins and it faces the town.
Reed's gone quiet. Come summer you can't normally hear yourself out here.
Sporantle coming up thick on the mud, thicker than I've ever had them, and it all goes in the back of the fare book where I keep that sort of thing.
The festival goes on the water here. Every boat lit at once.

The whole channel goes orange and then the year turns. Corbett sets the price, and we wait on the steps for the number that the town eats on. The dry end of the steps goes first, so people get down early.
Three re-cuts in six years, and I overdid the second.
Every net I've cut down is hanging in the shed on its own peg, oldest at the back. In the dark I can put my hand on the one I cut the year my son was born.
Not seen a Fenmaw on the channel run all this season.
I used to put two a month in the back of my fare book. Mirefin are right up under the boat now. Put the pole down on one this morning without meaning to.
